question: Explain DOM parsing, render tree construction, and script execution. What is the difference between <script>, <script async>, and <script defer>?
rubric: Explains HTML parsing into DOM tree and CSS parsing into CSSOM tree
Describes how DOM + CSSOM combine to form the Render Tree and Layout phase

Differentiates standard <script> (blocks parsing), async (fetches in parallel, executes immediately upon download blocking DOM), and defer (fetches in parallel, executes in order after DOM parsing completes)
Mentions DOMContentLoaded event timing relative to script loading
sampleAnswer:
When a browser requests an HTML document, it streams bytes and converts them to tokens, nodes, and the DOM tree in parallel with fetching external resources. In parallel, linked CSS files are parsed into the CSSOM. The browser combines DOM and CSSOM to create the Render Tree, which calculates layout dimensions and paints pixels.

Script Execution Modes:
1. Standard `<script>`: Pauses HTML parsing immediately, downloads the JS file synchronously, executes it, and then resumes HTML parsing. This blocks first contentful paint (FCP).
2. `<script async>`: Downloads the script asynchronously in parallel with HTML parsing. As soon as download finishes, HTML parsing pauses to execute the script immediately. Order of execution is non-deterministic.
3. `<script defer>`: Downloads the script asynchronously in parallel with HTML parsing, but delays execution until HTML parsing is fully complete (just before DOMContentLoaded). Preserves execution order.
codeSnippet:
<!-- Standard: Blocks parsing during download and execution -->
<script src="app.js"></script>

<!-- Async: Downloads parallel, pauses parsing to execute as soon as ready -->
<script async src="analytics.js"></script>

<!-- Defer: Downloads parallel, executes in DOM order after parsing finishes -->
<script defer src="main-bundle.js"></script>
commonPitfalls: Confusing async with defer regarding execution order
Assuming defer delays download rather than execution
Forgetting that async scripts execute out of order as soon as they finish downloading

question: How do <picture>, <source>, and srcset with sizes enable responsive media delivery and prevent layout shift?

sampleAnswer: Responsive images use two main patterns: 1. Resolution Switching (`srcset` + `sizes` on ``): Allows browser to choose the ideal image resolution based on device pixel ratio (DPR) and layout viewport width. The `sizes` attribute tells the preloader how wide the image will render before CSS loads. 2. Art Direction (`` element): Used when image crop or format (AVIF, WebP, JPEG) must change depending on viewport media queries or browser format support. To prevent CLS, always provide explicit `width` and `height` attributes on the `` tag so the browser computes the aspect-ratio slot before the image downloads.

question: Explain Block Formatting Context (BFC), Stacking Contexts (z-index), and Container Queries vs Media Queries.
rubric: Defines BFC and lists triggers (display: flow-root, overflow: hidden, flex/grid items, position: fixed/absolute)
Explains how BFC prevents margin collapsing and clears floats
Explains Stacking Context creation (position + z-index, opacity < 1, transform, filter, isolation: isolate)
Compares Container Queries (@container) targeting parent element width vs Media Queries (@media) targeting viewport width
sampleAnswer:
A Block Formatting Context (BFC) is an isolated visual layout region where child blocks are laid out vertically. Forming a BFC (e.g. via `display: flow-root`) contains internal floats without clearfix hacks and prevents vertical margins from collapsing with elements outside the BFC.

A Stacking Context determines rendering order along the Z-axis. Child elements with `z-index: 9999` will still render behind an element with `z-index: 1` if their parent belongs to a lower stacking context. Stacking contexts are formed by `isolation: isolate`, `opacity < 1`, `transform`, `filter`, or `position` with non-auto `z-index`.

Container Queries (`@container`) evaluate the size of a designated parent container rather than the browser viewport (`@media`), making modular component design truly context-aware when placed in sidebars, modals, or grid columns.
commonPitfalls: Assuming high z-index overrides parent stacking contexts
Using overflow: hidden solely to clear floats instead of display: flow-root

question: How do CSS Grid and Flexbox differ in terms of 1D vs 2D layout calculation algorithms?
rubric: Identifies Flexbox as 1D (content-driven layout along main/cross axis) vs Grid as 2D (layout-driven rows and columns)
Explains flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis sizing math
Explains grid-template-columns with minmax(), fr units, and auto-fit/auto-fill
sampleAnswer:
Flexbox is designed for 1-dimensional layouts (a single row or column at a time) where children drive the layout size based on content. CSS Grid is designed for 2-dimensional layouts where the parent container defines a structured grid coordinate system of rows and columns.

In Flexbox, space distribution is calculated via `flex-basis`, `flex-grow`, and `flex-shrink`. In CSS Grid, track sizing uses fractional units (`fr`) alongside dynamic functions like `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))` to create responsive layouts without media queries.
commonPitfalls: Using Flexbox with hardcoded width percentages when CSS Grid is better suited
Confusing auto-fit (stretches tracks to fill remaining space) with auto-fill (creates empty tracks)

question: Explain the JavaScript Event Loop, Call Stack, Microtask queue, and Macrotask queue with execution order examples.
rubric: Describes single-threaded call stack execution
Identifies Microtasks (Promise.then, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver)
Identifies Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI rendering)
Explains that ALL microtasks in the queue drain completely before the next macrotask or browser paint
sampleAnswer:
JavaScript runs on a single-threaded event loop. Code execution starts on the synchronous Call Stack. When asynchronous tasks complete, their callbacks enter queue structures:

1. Microtask Queue: Holds Promise reactions (`.then`), `queueMicrotask`, and `MutationObserver`. The Event Loop drains the ENTIRE microtask queue before moving to the next task or triggering a screen repaint.
2. Macrotask Queue: Holds `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, network I/O, and UI events. The Event Loop processes ONE macrotask, then drains all microtasks that were queued, then yields to rendering if necessary, then picks the next macrotask.
commonPitfalls: Believing setTimeout(fn, 0) executes immediately before Promises
Not realizing an infinite loop of microtasks will starve the event loop and freeze UI rendering

question: How do Closures and Garbage Collection work in V8? Give an example of a memory leak caused by uncleaned closures.
rubric: Defines Closure as a function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment
Explains V8 Mark-and-Sweep garbage collection and root reachability
Demonstrates closure memory leak (shared scope retainment)
sampleAnswer:
A closure is formed when an inner function retains references to variables in its outer lexical scope, even after the outer function has returned. V8 uses a Mark-and-Sweep garbage collector: objects are eligible for GC when they are no longer reachable from root objects.

In V8, functions in the same lexical parent scope share a single closure scope object. If one inner function holds a reference to a huge object, and another inner function is kept alive, the huge object CANNOT be garbage collected.
commonPitfalls: Assuming garbage collection cleans up unused local variables even if a sibling closure in the same scope remains referenced
Forgetting to detach event listeners or clear setInterval callbacks in SPA navigation

question: How does React Fiber reconciliation work? How do concurrent features like useTransition and useDeferredValue prioritize render lanes?
rubric: Explains Fiber architecture as a linked list tree representation supporting interruptible, incremental rendering
Differentiates Render Phase (pure, asynchronous, interruptible) vs Commit Phase (synchronous DOM mutation)
Explains Lane Priority System (Sync lane vs InputContinuous vs Transition lane)
Describes how useTransition yields control to high-priority user inputs
sampleAnswer:
React Fiber replaced the synchronous stack reconciler with a linked-list data structure where every component instance is a 'Fiber node'. Fiber allows React to split rendering work into small chunks, pause work to handle urgent user input, and resume or discard work as priorities change.

Two Main Phases:
1. Render Phase: React traverses Fiber nodes, calls component functions, and calculates diffs. This phase is pure, async, and can be interrupted or restarted.
2. Commit Phase: React synchronously applies calculated mutations to the DOM and fires layout effects.
commonPitfalls: Performing side effects inside the Render phase
Confusing useTransition (for state update triggers) with useDeferredValue (for wrapping received prop values)

question: Compare React Server Components (RSC) vs Client Components. What are the rules for serializability across boundaries?
rubric: Explains RSC execute purely on the server, zero client bundle size impact, direct DB access
Explains Client Components ('use client') run on server for SSR and hydrate on client for interactivity
Explains serializability rule: Props passed from Server Components to Client Components must be serializable
sampleAnswer:
React Server Components (RSC) execute exclusively on the server during build or request time. They never ship their JavaScript code to the browser, allowing direct access to databases with zero bundle overhead.

Client Components (marked with `'use client'`) render on the server to generate HTML (SSR) and hydrate on the client to enable state (`useState`), side effects (`useEffect`), and event handlers (`onClick`).
commonPitfalls: Adding 'use client' at the top of every file out of habit
Attempting to pass non-serializable functions as props from RSC to Client Components

question: Explain Discriminated Unions, Type Narrowing, conditional types, and how the 'infer' keyword extracts types in generic utility functions.
rubric: Defines Discriminated Union with a common literal property tag
Explains Type Narrowing via switch/if guards and exhaustiveness checking using 'never'
Explains Conditional Types (T extends U ? X : Y)
Explains 'infer' keyword for pattern matching and extracting internal types within conditional types
sampleAnswer:
A Discriminated Union is a union of object types that share a single common literal property (the 'discriminant'). TypeScript narrows the specific object shape inside control flow blocks based on checks against that discriminant.

Conditional Types take the form `T extends U ? X : Y`. When combined with the `infer` keyword, TypeScript can extract sub-types dynamically during type inference.
commonPitfalls: Using non-literal properties as union discriminants
Forgetting exhaustiveness checking with 'never' when handling API response unions

question: What is the difference between type assertions (as), type guards (is), and unknown vs any?
rubric: Explains 'any' disables type checking vs 'unknown' enforces type checking before usage
Explains Type Assertions ('as') force compiler override without runtime checks
Explains Custom Type Guard functions using 'param is Type' predicate syntax for safe runtime validation
sampleAnswer:
`any` opts out of type safety completely. `unknown` represents an unknown type safely: TypeScript forces developers to perform runtime validation or type narrowing before accessing properties.

Type Assertion (`val as MyType`) tells the compiler to trust the developer's type assignment, but performs ZERO runtime validation.

Type Guard (`function isUser(val: unknown): val is User`) performs actual runtime property validation and returns a boolean.
commonPitfalls: Using 'as MyType' for untrusted network payloads instead of validating schemas
Using 'any' as a quick fix for complex generic type errors

question: How do you build a fully accessible modal dialog (WCAG 2.2 AA compliant)? Detail keyboard focus traps and screen reader roles.
rubric: Identifies key ARIA attributes: role='dialog', aria-modal='true', aria-labelledby, aria-describedby
Explains Focus Management: move focus into dialog on open, trap focus within dialog, restore focus on close
Mentions key bindings: Escape key to dismiss dialog
Explains hiding background content via inert attribute on app root
sampleAnswer:
An accessible modal dialog requires precise ARIA semantics, focus management, and keyboard event handling to pass WCAG 2.2 AA standards.

1. Markup & Semantics: `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`.
2. Focus Management: Save activeElement reference on open. Intercept `Tab` and `Shift+Tab` to trap focus within modal. Listen for `Escape` to close and restore focus.
3. Background Invalidation: Set `inert` or `aria-hidden="true"` on the main application container while modal is active.

question: What are aria-live regions (polite vs assertive), and how do you announce dynamic SPA updates?

2. `aria-live="assertive"`: Screen readers interrupt current speech immediately for urgent updates.

question: Walk through diagnosing and optimizing Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) on a heavy e-commerce PDP.
rubric: Defines Core Web Vitals: LCP (< 2.5s), INP (< 200ms), CLS (< 0.1)
Diagnoses LCP bottlenecks: hero image optimization (fetchpriority='high', inline CSS, preloading)
Diagnoses INP bottlenecks: long tasks (>50ms) on main thread, yielding via scheduler.yield() or requestAnimationFrame
Diagnoses CLS bottlenecks: un-sized images, font swapping with size-adjust
sampleAnswer:
Core Web Vitals measure user-centric performance metrics:

1. LCP (Largest Contentful Paint - Goal < 2.5s): Set `fetchpriority="high"` on hero image, preload critical image URLs in HTML `<head>`, and serve AVIF/WebP over CDN.
2. INP (Interaction to Next Paint - Goal < 200ms): Break up long tasks (>50ms) into micro-tasks using `await scheduler.yield()`, move heavy non-UI processing to Web Workers.
3. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift - Goal < 0.1): Reserve CSS aspect-ratio bounding boxes or skeleton layout slots for async content.
commonPitfalls: Lazy loading the LCP hero image (loading='lazy' causes severe LCP regression)
Focusing exclusively on Lighthouse lab data instead of real user monitoring field data

question: Explain how bundler tree-shaking works (ES Modules vs CommonJS) and how to diagnose bundle bloat.
rubric: Explains Tree-Shaking as dead code elimination based on static import/export analysis
Explains why ES Modules enable static analysis vs CommonJS dynamic execution
Explains sideEffects flag in package.json
Tools: rollup-plugin-visualizer, webpack-bundle-analyzer
sampleAnswer:
Tree-shaking is a bundler optimization technique that removes unused exports from the production JavaScript bundle. It relies on ES Module (ESM) static syntax (`import` and `export`), where module dependencies can be analyzed at compile-time before code execution.

CommonJS (`require()`) calls are dynamic and can be evaluated inside conditional loops at runtime, making static dependency graph analysis and dead-code elimination impossible or unsafe.
commonPitfalls: Importing CJS versions of packages (e.g. lodash instead of lodash-es)
Top-level side effects inside unused modules preventing bundlers from safely pruning them

question: Explain how to debug a subtle async race condition where network responses return out of order, and how AbortController solves it.
rubric: Explains Async Race Condition scenario (stale response overwriting latest UI state)
Explains AbortController and AbortSignal for fetch cancellation
Explains integration with React useEffect cleanup
sampleAnswer:
An async race condition occurs when multiple asynchronous network requests are triggered sequentially, but complete out of order due to network latency variations.

Solution using `AbortController`: Before issuing a new fetch request, abort the previous pending request signal. This instantly cancels the in-flight HTTP request at the browser layer and prevents out-of-order state updates.

question: Compare git rebase vs git merge. When should you use interactive rebase (git rebase -i), and how do you resolve conflicts?
rubric: Compares git merge (non-destructive 3-way merge commit) vs git rebase (re-applies commits on top of tip)
Explains Interactive Rebase (`git rebase -i HEAD~N`): squash, reword, fixup, drop
Steps to resolve conflicts during rebase (`git add .` -> `git rebase --continue`)
sampleAnswer:
`git merge` combines two feature branches by creating a new 'merge commit'. It is non-destructive and preserves complete historical context.

`git rebase` rewrites history by taking commits from your feature branch and re-applying them sequentially onto the tip of the target base branch.

Interactive Rebase (`git rebase -i HEAD~N`) allows engineers to clean up local feature branches (squash typos, reword messages) before submitting a PR.
codeSnippet:
# Interactive rebase for last 4 commits
git rebase -i HEAD~4

# Resolve conflict workflow:
git add src/components/Dashboard.tsx
git rebase --continue
commonPitfalls: Rebasing public shared branches that teammates are actively pulling from
Using 'git push -f' without '--force-with-lease'

question: How does git bisect use binary search to locate regression bugs across a large codebase commit history?
rubric: Explains binary search algorithm applied to commit graph
Outlines manual bisect workflow: git bisect start -> git bisect bad -> git bisect good <commit>

sampleAnswer:
`git bisect` is a built-in debugging tool that uses binary search to find the exact commit that introduced a bug or performance regression in a codebase.

Workflow:
1. Initialize: `git bisect start`
2. Mark current broken commit as bad: `git bisect bad`
3. Mark historical working commit as good: `git bisect good v1.2.0`
4. Git automatically checks out a commit halfway. You test, mark good/bad, and Git isolates the culprit commit.
codeSnippet:
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v2.4.0
git bisect run npm test -- --spec src/tests/cart.test.ts

question: Walk through how you'd test a component that fetches data from an API on mount, covering loading, error, and success states. What would you mock, and what would you leave real?
rubric: Identifies this as an integration test spanning the component, its data-fetching logic, and the network boundary
Proposes mocking only the network call (e.g. via MSW) rather than the component's internal fetch logic
Covers all three states explicitly: loading, error, and success -- not just the happy path
Uses role/text-based queries (React Testing Library conventions) rather than querying internal state or CSS classes
sampleAnswer:
I'd treat this as an integration test. I'd use MSW to intercept the actual network request and control what it returns, while letting the component's real fetch logic, state management, and rendering run unmodified -- mocking the fetch function directly would test less of the real code path.

For each state I'd render the component under a different MSW handler: one that delays or never resolves (loading state, asserting a loading indicator appears), one that returns an error status (asserting an error message with a retry option renders), and one that returns valid data (asserting the actual content renders). I'd query everything the way a user would -- getByRole, getByText -- not by reaching into component internals.
commonPitfalls: Only testing the success path and skipping loading/error states entirely
Mocking the component's own fetch wrapper instead of the network boundary, which tests less of the real integration
Querying by CSS class or test id instead of role/text, coupling the test to markup instead of behavior
followUpQuestions: How would this test differ if you were unit-testing a validation function used by the same component?

question: What's the difference between a unit test, a component test, and an integration test, and how would you decide which one a given piece of new code needs?
rubric: Defines a unit test as isolated logic testing (typically a pure function), no DOM or rendering involved
Defines a component test as rendering a single component and asserting on user-visible output
Defines an integration test as multiple real units (components, hooks, logic) working together, usually with only the network boundary mocked
Gives a concrete decision heuristic, e.g. pure logic -> unit, isolated UI behavior -> component, cross-piece wiring -> integration
sampleAnswer:
A unit test checks one isolated piece of logic, usually a pure function, with no rendering involved -- fast and precise. A component test renders a single component and asserts on what a user would see, querying by role or text rather than internals. An integration test exercises multiple real pieces together -- a form, its validation, and a submit handler, for example -- with only the true external boundary (usually the network) mocked.

My rule of thumb: if it's pure logic with no side effects, unit test it directly. If it's one component's rendering behavior in isolation, component test it. If the value is in verifying that several real pieces actually work together correctly, that's an integration test -- and I try not to over-mock it, since mocking the thing you're trying to verify defeats the point.
commonPitfalls: Treating every test as an integration test, making the suite slow and hard to debug when something fails
Mocking so much in an 'integration' test that it no longer verifies real integration
Not extracting pure logic into testable functions, forcing everything through slower component-level tests

question: A teammate wants to store the app's JWT in localStorage because it's simpler to read and attach to requests manually. What's your concern, and what would you propose instead?
rubric: Explains that localStorage is readable by any JavaScript on the page, including an attacker's script from any XSS vulnerability
Proposes an httpOnly cookie as the alternative, explaining that it's invisible to JavaScript entirely
Identifies the tradeoff: cookie-based auth reopens a CSRF consideration that manually-attached tokens didn't have
Mentions Secure and SameSite flags as part of a properly configured solution, not just httpOnly alone
sampleAnswer:
My concern is that any XSS vulnerability anywhere on the site -- even in a third-party script -- gives an attacker a trivial way to read the token straight out of localStorage and take over the account. I'd propose storing the token in an httpOnly cookie instead, since JavaScript can't read it at all, closing that vector completely.

The tradeoff is that cookies are automatically attached to requests by the browser, which reopens CSRF as a consideration in a way manually-attached localStorage tokens didn't have. So I wouldn't treat httpOnly as sufficient on its own -- I'd pair it with Secure (HTTPS-only) and SameSite (restricting cross-site sending), and depending on the app, a CSRF token for state-changing requests too.
codeSnippet: Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict
commonPitfalls: Treating httpOnly cookies as a strictly safer drop-in replacement without addressing the CSRF tradeoff they introduce
Forgetting the Secure flag, allowing the cookie over plaintext HTTP
Assuming client-side token expiration checks are a security measure rather than a UX convenience
followUpQuestions: How would you explain the CSRF risk to someone who thinks 'the cookie has HttpOnly so we're safe'?
What would you check first if you suspected an XSS vulnerability was already present in the app?

question: What's the difference between what the same-origin policy protects against and what CORS actually does? Why doesn't the same-origin policy alone prevent CSRF?
rubric: Explains the same-origin policy as the browser's default restriction blocking cross-origin JavaScript from reading a response
Explains CORS as a server-controlled, opt-in exception to that default restriction via response headers
Explains that CSRF doesn't need to read the response -- a forged form submission or image request can still cause damage (e.g. a state change) without the attacker seeing anything back
Distinguishes this from an authorization failure -- a CORS error means the request succeeded but the browser blocked read access to it
sampleAnswer:
The same-origin policy is the browser's default: JavaScript on one origin can't read the response of a request to a different origin. CORS is the mechanism a server uses to explicitly opt certain origins into being allowed to read its responses, via response headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

CSRF isn't prevented by the same-origin policy because a forged request doesn't need to read the response to cause harm -- a form auto-submitted from a malicious site can trigger a state-changing action like a funds transfer, and the browser still attaches the user's real cookies to it automatically. The same-origin policy blocks the attacker from seeing the result, but the damage is already done by the time that would matter.
commonPitfalls: Confusing a CORS error with a 401/403 authorization failure -- they're different things at different layers
Assuming CORS headers protect against CSRF, when they address a different problem (read access to responses, not the request being sent at all)
Believing the same-origin policy alone is sufficient CSRF protection
followUpQuestions: What triggers a CORS preflight request, and why does it exist?
How would SameSite cookies close the gap the same-origin policy leaves open for CSRF?

question: Explain the difference between a Server Component and a Client Component in Next.js's App Router, and how you'd decide where to draw that boundary in a real page.
rubric: Explains Server Components render only on the server and never ship code to the browser, including their imports
Explains why hooks and browser APIs don't work in Server Components -- there's no browser runtime to attach to
Explains 'use client' as an explicit opt-in for a specific component that needs interactivity, state, or browser APIs
Gives a concrete strategy: extract only the genuinely interactive piece into a small Client Component rather than marking a whole page 'use client'
sampleAnswer:
Every component in the App Router is a Server Component by default -- it renders entirely on the server, and its code, including anything it imports, never reaches the browser. That's why hooks like useState don't work there: there's no browser runtime to track state and re-render against. A Client Component, marked with 'use client', opts into running in the browser, which is what you need for interactivity, state, or browser APIs.

In a real page, I try to keep as much as possible as Server Components -- for the SEO and bundle-size benefits -- and only extract the specific interactive piece, like a 'like' button or a form, into its own small Client Component. Marking an entire page 'use client' just to support one button pulls everything else in that file back into client-rendered territory unnecessarily.
commonPitfalls: Adding 'use client' to an entire page to fix one small interactive element, losing server-rendering benefits for the whole file
Trying to use useState or useEffect inside a Server Component
Assuming Server Components can't fetch data -- they can, directly, without useEffect
followUpQuestions: How does data fetching differ between a Server Component and a Client Component?
When would you still need a Route Handler instead of a Server Action?

question: How would you choose between SSR, SSG, and ISR for a given page, and how does that choice affect Core Web Vitals?
rubric: Defines SSR (per-request rendering), SSG (build-time rendering), and ISR (static with periodic background regeneration)
Ties the choice to the page's actual freshness and traffic needs, not a one-size-fits-all default
Connects the choice to LCP specifically -- pre-rendered HTML (SSG/ISR) typically arrives and paints faster than per-request SSR or client-rendered pages
Mentions that different routes in the same app can use different strategies
sampleAnswer:
SSR renders fresh HTML per request, which is right for content that must be current on every load but costs server compute per request. SSG renders once at build time and serves a static file to everyone, which is extremely fast and cheap but only as fresh as the last build -- good for content like marketing pages that rarely changes. ISR is the middle ground: statically generated, but regenerated periodically in the background, which fits something like a product page that updates a few times a day under high traffic.

For Core Web Vitals, SSG and ISR routes typically get the best LCP since the HTML arrives already rendered -- there's no per-request server work blocking the first paint. I'd pick per-route: a dashboard that needs live data might stay SSR or fully dynamic, while the marketing pages around it are SSG, all in the same app.
codeSnippet:
// Opting a specific route into full per-request rendering
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';
commonPitfalls: Assuming the whole app must use one rendering strategy
Choosing SSR by default for pages that don't actually need per-request freshness, adding unnecessary server cost
Not considering ISR as a middle ground between full SSG and full SSR
followUpQuestions: How would Suspense and streaming change your answer for a page with one slow, non-critical data dependency?
How do Server Components affect the amount of JavaScript shipped, independent of the rendering strategy chosen?

question: What's the difference between the defer and async attributes on a <script> tag, and when would you use each?
rubric: Explains that both let the script download without blocking HTML parsing
Explains defer executes scripts in order, after parsing completes
Explains async executes as soon as the script downloads, in arbitrary order relative to other scripts, potentially before parsing finishes
Gives a concrete use case for each
sampleAnswer: Both defer and async let the browser download the script without blocking HTML parsing, but they differ in when and how the script actually runs. defer waits until parsing is completely finished, then runs scripts in their original document order -- good for scripts that depend on the DOM being ready and on each other's order, like most application bundles. async runs the script as soon as it finishes downloading, independent of parsing and independent of other async scripts' order -- good for independent scripts like analytics that don't need to coordinate with anything else on the page.
codeSnippet:
<script src="analytics.js" async></script>
<script src="app-bundle.js" defer></script>
commonPitfalls: Assuming async and defer are interchangeable
Using async for scripts that depend on DOM elements or execution order
followUpQuestions: What happens to a normal <script> tag with neither attribute?
Where would you place a script that needs to run before any HTML renders?

question: Explain CSS specificity and walk through how you'd resolve a conflict where a utility class isn't overriding a component's own styles.
rubric: Correctly orders specificity: inline styles > ids > classes/attributes/pseudo-classes > elements
Explains source order only breaks ties between selectors of equal specificity
Diagnoses that a longer, multi-class chained selector often beats a single utility class
Prefers a structural fix (matching specificity or reducing component selector nesting) over reaching for !important
sampleAnswer:
Specificity is calculated per selector, roughly: inline styles beat IDs, which beat classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, which beat plain element selectors. Source order only decides ties when two selectors have equal specificity -- a later, lower-specificity rule never overrides an earlier, higher-specificity one just because it loads after.

If a utility class like .text-danger isn't applying, I'd check what it's actually competing against -- often it's a deeply chained component selector like .card .btn.btn-primary, which has higher specificity than a single class. My first instinct isn't !important, since that just creates the next override problem -- I'd either match specificity deliberately or, longer-term, keep component styles from accumulating multi-class chained selectors that make simple utility overrides hard in the first place.
codeSnippet:
.card .btn.btn-primary { color: white; } /* higher specificity, wins */
.text-danger { color: red; } /* loses, regardless of load order */
commonPitfalls: Assuming later-loaded CSS always wins
Reaching for !important as a first fix rather than a last resort
followUpQuestions: How would you design a utility-class system to avoid these conflicts in the first place?
What's the specificity of an ID selector combined with a class?

question: What's a closure, and can you give a practical example of where you'd deliberately use one?
rubric: Defines a closure as a function retaining access to its enclosing scope's variables after that scope has returned
Gives a concrete, correct example (counter factory, memoization cache, event handler capturing a value)
Explains why this differs from the variable simply being global
sampleAnswer: A closure is a function that keeps access to variables from the scope it was created in, even after that outer function has already finished running. A practical example is a counter factory: createCounter() returns an increment function that keeps its own private count variable alive across calls, without that variable being global or accessible from outside. Each call to createCounter() produces an independent counter with its own closure over a separate count.
commonPitfalls: Confusing a closure with simply using a global variable
Not realizing each call to the outer function creates a distinct closure
followUpQuestions: How do closures relate to the stale closure bug common in React's useEffect?
What's a memory consideration when closures capture large objects?

question: Why does React require hooks to be called unconditionally, in the same order, on every render?
rubric: Explains React tracks hooks by call order/index across renders, not by name
Explains that a conditional hook call shifts that order, misaligning state between hooks on subsequent renders
Gives an example of the resulting bug (wrong state value attached to the wrong hook)
sampleAnswer: React tracks each component's hooks by the order they're called in, not by name or any other identifier -- internally it's essentially a list indexed by call order. If a hook call is wrapped in a condition that can differ between renders, the call order shifts on renders where the condition differs, which misaligns every hook after it with the wrong stored state. That's why hooks have to be called unconditionally at the top level, in the same order, every single render -- conditionals need to go inside the hook (like inside a useEffect's callback), not around the hook call itself.
commonPitfalls: Putting a hook call inside an if statement or early return
Calling hooks inside loops with a variable iteration count
followUpQuestions: What ESLint rule catches this class of mistake automatically?
How would you conditionally skip logic inside a useEffect without skipping the hook call itself?

question: What's a discriminated union, and why is it a common pattern for modeling async request state?
rubric: Defines a discriminated union as a union of object types sharing a common literal field
Explains that field lets TypeScript narrow reliably by switching on it
Applies it concretely to loading/error/success request state
sampleAnswer: A discriminated union is a union of object shapes that all share one common literal field -- often called status or kind -- which TypeScript can switch on to narrow reliably to the right variant. For async request state, it's a much safer alternative to separate boolean flags like isLoading/isError/isSuccess, which can end up in impossible or contradictory combinations. With a discriminated union, only one state is representable at a time, and switching on status gives you fully type-safe access to state-specific fields, like an error message that only exists on the error variant.
commonPitfalls: Modeling request state as several independent booleans instead of one discriminated union
Forgetting the shared literal field, which breaks TypeScript's ability to narrow
followUpQuestions: How would you exhaustively check that every variant of the union is handled in a switch statement?
What's the risk of using separate boolean flags instead?

question: How would you make a custom dropdown menu (built from divs, not a native <select>) accessible to keyboard and screen reader users?
rubric: Identifies the need for real keyboard support (Tab, Enter/Space to open, arrow keys to navigate, Escape to close)
Mentions appropriate ARIA roles (e.g. role="listbox"/"option" or a native <button> trigger)
Mentions focus management -- moving focus into the open menu and back to the trigger on close
Prefers a native element or well-tested pattern over hand-rolling ARIA where possible
sampleAnswer: First, I'd check whether a native <select> or an existing accessible library component could do the job -- reinventing this well is genuinely hard. If a custom implementation is truly necessary, I'd make sure the trigger is a real <button>, add appropriate ARIA (role="listbox" and role="option" on the items, aria-expanded on the trigger), and implement full keyboard support: Enter/Space to open, arrow keys to move between options, Enter to select, and Escape to close. I'd also manage focus explicitly -- moving it into the open menu, and back to the trigger button when it closes -- since none of that happens automatically for a custom widget the way it does for a native select.
codeSnippet:
{isOpen && (
    {options.map(o =>
  • {o.label}
    • )}
)}
commonPitfalls: Building a visually correct dropdown with zero keyboard support
Forgetting to manage focus on open/close
Missing ARIA roles that communicate the widget's structure to screen readers
followUpQuestions: Why is reaching for a native element usually better than a custom ARIA implementation?
How would you test this component's accessibility beyond an automated scanner?

question: You're handed a minified production stack trace with no useful information. Walk through how you'd actually debug it.
rubric: Mentions source maps as the mechanism to de-minify a production trace
Describes checking the error tracking tool for the de-minified version before anything else
Describes attempting to reproduce locally with the same inputs/conditions
Describes isolating which frames are in your own code vs. a dependency
sampleAnswer: First I'd check whether the error tracking tool already has source maps uploaded and can show me a de-minified trace -- that's usually the fastest path to a real file and line number. If that's not available, I'd try to reproduce the issue locally against the same build config, since a local unminified trace should point to the same underlying bug. Once I have a readable trace, I'd separate which frames are actually in my own code versus a library, since a dependency's internal frames are rarely where the real fix belongs. From there it's normal debugging: understanding what the error type and message actually indicate, not just where it happened.
commonPitfalls: Trying to debug directly from a minified trace without checking for source maps first
Assuming the deepest stack frame is always where the real bug is, even when it's inside a third-party library
followUpQuestions: Why might source maps be intentionally excluded from a production build, and how would you handle that tradeoff?
How would you approach an error that only reproduces in production, not locally?

question: When would you choose git rebase over git merge, and what real risk does rebase carry that merge doesn't?
rubric: Explains rebase produces a linear history by replaying commits; merge preserves both branches' actual history
Gives a reasonable use case for each (rebase for cleaning up a local feature branch before opening a PR; merge for integrating shared/public branches)
Identifies the core risk: rebasing commits that have already been pushed/shared rewrites history other people may already be building on
sampleAnswer:
I'd reach for rebase to clean up my own local feature branch before opening a PR -- squashing exploratory commits into something coherent, with a linear history that's easier to review. I'd use merge when integrating shared branches, like merging a feature branch into main, since it preserves the actual history of both branches without rewriting anything.

The real risk with rebase is rewriting history that other people have already pulled and built on -- if you rebase a branch someone else has based work on, their history and yours diverge in a way that creates a genuinely messy, hard-to-reconcile conflict. As a rule, I don't rebase anything that's already been pushed and shared, only my own local, not-yet-shared commits.
codeSnippet:
git checkout feature-branch
git rebase -i main   # clean up local history before opening a PR
# vs.
git checkout main
git merge feature-branch   # integrate a shared branch, preserving history
commonPitfalls: Rebasing a branch that others have already pulled from
Force-pushing after a rebase without communicating to collaborators
followUpQuestions: What would you do if you'd already rebased a shared branch and a teammate is now stuck with a broken history?
What does git rebase --onto do?

question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision made by a teammate or your team. How did you handle it?
rubric: Describes a specific, real technical disagreement rather than a vague generality
Explains how they raised the concern constructively rather than dismissing the other person's approach
Describes the actual outcome, including if the resolution wasn't fully in their favor
Reflects on what they'd do differently, if anything
sampleAnswer: In a past project, a teammate wanted to add a new state management library for a feature I thought could be handled with existing patterns already in the codebase. Instead of just pushing back in a meeting, I asked to understand their reasoning first -- it turned out they were solving for a specific cross-component sync issue I hadn't fully considered. I proposed we prototype both approaches quickly and compare, rather than debate it abstractly. The prototype showed their approach genuinely solved the sync issue more cleanly, so we went with it -- but we also agreed to document the decision so the next person wouldn't have to re-litigate it. I try to treat disagreements as something to resolve with evidence, not persuasion.
commonPitfalls: Describing a disagreement with no concrete resolution or outcome
Framing it as being 'right' rather than reaching a good decision together
followUpQuestions: What would you have done if the prototype comparison had been inconclusive?
How do you handle a disagreement with someone more senior than you?

question: What's the difference between authentication and authorization, and how does that distinction show up in a real bug you might see in code review?
rubric: Correctly defines authentication as verifying identity, authorization as verifying permission
Gives a concrete example of an authorization bug distinct from an authentication bug
Notes that both need to be enforced server-side, not just reflected in the UI
sampleAnswer: Authentication answers 'who are you' -- verifying identity, typically via login. Authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do' -- verifying permission for a specific action, once identity is already known. A common real bug: an app correctly authenticates a user but then only hides an admin-only button in the UI for non-admins, without checking permission server-side on the actual admin API endpoint. That's an authorization gap -- any authenticated user could call the endpoint directly and bypass the UI-level restriction entirely.
commonPitfalls: Confusing the two terms
Relying on hiding a UI element as the only access control
followUpQuestions: How would you fix the authorization gap in the example?
What's the difference between role-based and attribute-based access control?

question: How would you approach adding tests to an existing feature that currently has zero test coverage, without blocking on rewriting the whole thing?
rubric: Suggests starting with the highest-risk or most-changed code paths rather than attempting full coverage at once
Suggests extracting pure logic into testable functions where reasonable, rather than testing everything through the UI
Mentions writing a test for the next bug fix as a practical, incremental habit
Doesn't propose a full rewrite as a prerequisite to testing
sampleAnswer: I wouldn't try to reach full coverage in one pass -- I'd start with the highest-risk or most frequently changed parts of the feature, since that's where regressions are most likely and most costly. Where there's business logic tangled up in a component, I'd look for opportunities to extract it into pure, testable functions rather than testing everything indirectly through rendering. And practically, I'd adopt a habit of writing a test alongside every bug fix in that area going forward, so coverage grows incrementally instead of needing a dedicated, hard-to-justify 'add tests' project.
commonPitfalls: Treating 'add tests' as requiring a full rewrite first
Trying to reach 100% coverage immediately instead of prioritizing by risk
followUpQuestions: How would you convince a team to invest time in this when there's constant feature pressure?
What would you test first in a checkout flow with zero coverage?
